title: X (Twitter): Sign In With X and Post From Workflows

chapters.title: X (Twitter) in Orchard Core
chapters.subtitle: Sign in with X, and post from workflows

steps.text: The X (Twitter) module connects your site to X in two ways. Visitors can sign in with their X account, and a workflow can post to X when something happens on your site. In this video, we'll set up both.

chapters.title: What the module provides
chapters.subtitle: Two features and one X app

steps.text: The module has two features. X (Twitter) Integration stores the keys of your X app, and, when Workflows is enabled, adds a workflow task that posts to X. Sign in with X (Twitter) adds a button to the login page.

Both rely on an app that you create on the X developer platform. Its Keys and tokens tab provides the four values the module asks for: the API key, the API secret key, the Access Token, and the Access Token Secret.
Let's open Tools, Features, and search for Twitter. The module has two features, listed under the X (Twitter) category.
Sign in with X (Twitter) lists X (Twitter) Integration and External Authentication as its dependencies. Let's enable it.
Enabling a feature also enables its dependencies, so both X (Twitter) features show Enabled. Their settings pages are in the Settings menu.

chapters.title: Enter the keys of your X app
chapters.subtitle: Settings, Integrations, X (Twitter)

steps.text: Open Settings, Integrations, X (Twitter). As the warning at the top of the page says, saving these settings might restart the site.
Enter the API key and the Access Token from the Keys and tokens tab of your app. Both fields are marked as required.
The API secret key and the Access Token Secret are password fields, so their values show as dots. Enter both: with any of the four values missing, the login page shows no X button.
Select Save. The page confirms that the site settings are updated, and the two secret fields tell you that the value is securely stored.
If the Secrets feature is enabled, each secret field can instead use a secret kept in the Secrets module. A separate video covers that feature.

chapters.title: Set up Sign in with X
chapters.subtitle: Callback path and tokens

steps.text: Open Settings, Security, Authentication, Sign In with X (Twitter). The keys come from the integration settings, so this page has only two options.
The CallbackPath is where X returns visitors to your site after they sign in. Enter /signin-x, and set the callback URL of your X app to your site's address followed by the same path.
Store tokens saves the external authentication tokens for reuse, and we leave it cleared. Select Save, and the site might restart to apply the settings.
Let's open the login page. Next to the usual Log in form, a section titled Use another service to log in offers the X (Twitter) button.
Selecting the button sends the visitor to X to sign in. X then returns the visitor to the callback path of your site.
When X returns a visitor, the site looks for an account already linked to that X account. If it finds one and that account is allowed to sign in, the visitor is signed in.

Otherwise, if X provides an email that matches a local account, the page Link your account asks for that account's password. If not, the page Create a new account opens, unless the external registration settings disable new registrations or create accounts without asking.
A signed-in user can also add X to an account later, from External Logins in the user menu.
The module adds a task to Workflows, which is enabled on this site. Let's open Design, Workflows, select Create Workflow, enter a name, and select Create and open the designer.
An empty workflow offers the events to start with. We pick Content Published Event, and the designer marks it as the start activity.
In its settings, Content Types limits the event to the types you choose. We pick Blog Post, so other content does not run the workflow.
Point at the Done outcome until a plus appears, select it, and search for Twitter. Update X (Twitter) Status Task is listed under Social, and the designer adds it already connected.
Its settings include Template for updating X (Twitter) status, the text of the post. The field is required, so the activity shows an issue until you enter text and leave the field.
The task has two outcomes. Done follows when X accepts the post, and Failed follows when X returns an error.
The designer keeps your changes as a draft, and a draft does not run. Select Publish, and from then on publishing a Blog Post sends the text to X.
With the keys of your X app saved, visitors can sign in with X, and workflows can post to X. Thanks for watching.
